Group member names: Ahlyn (Ashley) Kim, Wareesha Saeed, Alexis Magana

Collins Hill High School, Suwanee, GA 
 
Plant Mars Challenge, Spring 2026, High School Division

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 2 
Introduction 
​
Sending humans to Mars for long periods of time creates many challenges, especially 
when it comes to providing fresh food. Astronauts cannot rely only on packaged meals from 
Earth because of the limited amount and the lack of nutrients over time. Because of this, 
scientists are studying how to grow plants in space, specifically Mars. One of the biggest 
challenges is that Martian soil does not contain the nutrients and organic materials that plants 
need to grow. It is dry, crusty and lacks nitrogen, which is one of the most important nutrients for 
plant growth. The purpose of this experiment will help test what type and amount of fertilizers 
could help plants grow in soil similar to Martian conditions by focusing on comparing organic 
and synthetic fertilizers. In comparison, synthetic fertilizers are made by humans and usually 
provide nutrients more quickly and in higher amounts. The experiment tested two different 
amounts, 25 mL and 50 mL, to see how both the type and amount of fertilizer affected growth. 
​
Green beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) were chosen for this experiment because of the several 
qualities that make them useful for Mars farming. First, green beans are classified as legumes 
which means they can take nitrogen from the air and turn it into nutrients in the soil through a 
natural process. This is very important because Martian soil does not have the nitrogen that can 
be used to support plant life. Green beans also grow relatively fast and do not need a large 
amount of space, making them reasonable for small growing areas like on a spacecraft or a Mars 
base. Another reason green beans were chosen is because they are known to grow in difficult 
environments, including volcanic soils that are similar to Martian soil. Volcanic soil shares some 
features with Martian soil such as low nutrients and rough texture. This suggests that green beans 
may be able to adapt to Martian conditions better than other plants.

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 3 
​
An important benefit of growing plants like green beans during missions like to Mars is 
the positive effect on astronauts' mental health. Living in space or on Mars far away from home 
can be stressful and isolating as they are far from family, surrounded by a small crew, and stuck 
in a limited space for a long period of time. This can cause the crew to experience loneliness, 
anxiety and boredom. Taking care of plants can help reduce these feelings by giving astronauts a 
daily task that makes them feel more at home. Watching plants grow over time can help 
astronauts feel a sense of progress and accomplishment, which is important for maintaining a 
positive mindset. The color, smell and even the presence of plants can remind astronauts of 
Earth. 
​
This experiment is important because it helps show how green beans react to different 
conditions in a controlled environment that is meant to be similar to Mars. The results showed 
that the plants grown with organic fertilizer had better growth than those with synthetic 
fertilizers. The plants with synthetic fertilizers did not grow at all. One possible reason for this is 
that synthetic fertilizers might have provided too much of certain nutrients, especially nitrogen, 
which could harm the roots instead of helping them. Since green beans already produce their 
own nitrogen, adding too much nitrogen may have affected their natural growth negatively. On 
the other hand, organic fertilizers may have helped the green beans grow by improving the soil 
slowly and safely. Organic fertilizers often make the soil better at holding water and supporting 
helpful microorganisms, which are tiny living things that help plants grow. Even though worms 
were added to improve the soil, most of them did not survive, which suggested that the soil 
conditions were not good. This shows that more work is needed to create a soil environment that 
can support both plants and other living organisms on Mars.

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 4 
In conclusion, this experiment provides useful information about how to grow green 
beans on Mars. It shows that choosing the right type of fertilizer is very important. The findings 
could help scientists and engineers design better farming systems for future missions to Mars. In 
the future, testing different fertilizers, changing the amount given or trying other plants could 
help improve results even more. This helps successfully grow food on Mars and help support 
human life on Mars. 
Experimental Design 
For the PBL Project, the scientists began their experiment in a science lab located in 
Collins Hill High School. These scientists had to follow very strict protocols not only for their 
safety but also for others. These protocols were safety procedures such as safety goggles, masks 
and gloves provided by The Institute of Competition Sciences. Martian regolith or Martian dust 
is considered very toxic and poisonous to humans. If it makes contact with the eyes, nose and/or 
mouth, it can cause severe irritation and/or respiratory and internal risks. Also, due to their high 
toxic components and the fact that Martian dust is very fine, inhalation and ingestion can cause 
the dust particles to be lodged into the lungs and/or absorbed into the bloodstream. According to 
PubMed Central, “Toxic components of martian dust include perchlorates, silica, nanophase iron 
oxides, and gypsum in addition to trace amounts of toxic metals whose abundances are debated: 
chromium, beryllium, arsenic, and cadmium.” 
​
In addition to their growth advantages, green beans could play an important role in 
creating a closed-loop life, a lifestyle that is designed to mimic nature, a support system for long 
term space missions. In environments like a Mars base, waste recycling is essential because 
resources are extremely limited. Green bean plants can be set up into systems where organic 
waste, such as plant scraps and safely processed human waste, is broken down and reused as

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 5 
nutrients for future crops. This reduces the need to transport large amounts of fertilizer from 
Earth. Also advanced plant growth habitats are designed to carefully control light cycles during 
LED technology, regulate humidity and recycle water through condensation systems. According 
to NASA, “Future plant research conducted in these research facilities will help enable 
exploration by improving our understanding of how plants, their associated microbiomes in 
leaves and roots, and how they grow in the spaceflight environment.” This shows that growing 
plants in space is not just about food production, but also understanding the relationship between 
plants and their microscopic friends. Green beans could be benefitted because they naturally 
form relationships with bacteria that help them obtain nitrogen and grow in poor soil conditions. 
By studying the interactions, scientists can design better growing systems for Mars that could 
help support both plants and beneficial microorganisms. Lastly, studies conducted on the ISS 
have also shown that tending plants could help improve crew cooperation and provide a 
responsibility they all share. This helps strengthen team work and trust. These additional benefits 
show that green beans are not just a food source but also a key part of a sustainable living space 
on Mars. 
Methods 
​
The research conducted before planting explored the differences between organic and 
synthetic fertilizers, and their effects on both the growth of a plant and the quality of the soil. 
This was conducted while minding the effects of the Martian soil combined with the potting mix. 
With this, the hypothesis was then able to be furtherly curated and condensed into one final 
statement: Different amounts of synthetic and organic fertilizers will affect the growth rates and 
lengths of green beans when observed. Findings suggested that synthetic fertilizers produced 
with nutrient boosting chemicals contribute to damaged and dry soil but offered large growth

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 6 
results (Cherlinka 2024). In contrast, organic fertilizers containing different microbes that shared 
a symbiotic relationship the soil were suggested to be a healthier alternative for both the plant 
and the soil (Cherlinka 2024). Given to the researchers by the competition hosts were 5 medium 
sized pots, black latex gloves, a variety of seeds to choose from, and a large container of Martian 
soil simulant. Teachers and educators provided other seed options, purified water, potting mix, 
UV lamps to simulate sunlight, worms, and aluminum trays large enough to fit all 5 pots. 
Different variables of influence were controlled by researchers in order to ensure fullest 
potential success. Independent variables such as the amount and type of fertilizer were never 
modified during the experiment as it would affect the results of the data. For the synthetic 
fertilizer, Miracle-Gro LiquaFeed All Purpose Plant Food was used which contained a 12-4-8 
ratio of nitrogen, phosphate, and potassium as observed in the manufacturing label. This product 
was chosen to represent the synthetic fertilizer as it contained chemicals and man-made 
ingredients that promoted instantaneous growth by feeding the plant. This contrasts the organic 
fertilizer used, Mykos Pure Mycorrhizal Inoculant, as the microbial activity feeds the soil which 
then provides nutrients for the plant to grow. As for the dependent variable, the growth of the 
plant was observed over the course of 8 weeks as the data recorded height in inches, new 
growths such as leaves, and irregularities caused by environmental stresses such as changes in 
stem and leaf texture. Controlled environmental elements were crucial in maintaining a stable 
environment for the legumes to grow. All 5 pots were placed in an aluminum tray to be grouped 
together and placed on a table two feet away from a UV light source that remained powered on 
for the entire duration of the experiment. Within the pots was a mixture of 300 milliliters of 
Martian soil simulant and 300 milliliters of potting mix to create a 50:50 ratio. Each pot was 
filled with the soil mixture approximately 85% from the top of the pot. No modifications were

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 7 
made to the amount of potting mix nor the amount of Martian soil simulant. Additionally, one 
earthworm was administered to each pot and left to maintain sufficient nutritional balance. 50 
milliliters of water were added to each pot every day along with light misting from a plastic 
spray bottle. Approximately 4-5 sprays were used to mist all 5 plants along with the 50 milliliters 
of water given. 
All materials utilized are listed below: 
●​ 5 medium sized pots 
●​ 1 medium sized aluminum tray 
●​ Table/stand 
●​ UV lamp 
●​ Potting mix 
●​ Simulated Martian soil 
●​ Purified water 
●​ 5 green bean seeds 
●​ Miracle-Gro LiquaFeed All Purpose Plant Food 
●​ Mykos Pure Mycorrhizal Inoculant 
●​ Plant stabilizers for stem support 
●​ Graduated cylinder 
●​ Beaker 
●​ Pot labels 
​
Steps in order to replicate experiment: 
​
To begin, gather all ingredients listed above. Using a beaker, measure 300 milliliters of 
both the potting mix and the Martian soil and mix together. Take all 5 pots and fill each

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 8 
approximately until 85% full. Dedicate two pots to contain organic fertilizer and another two to 
contain synthetic fertilizer. The 5th pot will not contain any fertilizer. In the organic fertilizer 
pots, add 25 milliliters of Mykos Pure Mycorrhizal Inoculant in one pot and 50 milliliters in 
another. Mix and label accordingly. Repeat the steps for the synthetic fertilizer pots using 
Miracle-Gro LiquaFeed All Purpose Plant Food. In the middle of the mix, dig a small hole about 
an inch deep and insert one seed into each pot. Cover the seed with the mix in the pot and lightly 
pat down the soil and compact it. Gather all labeled pots and place them in an aluminum tray and 
on a table two feet away from the powered UV light.

​
For the first 3 weeks, it can be observed that the growth of 25 ml organic, 50 ml organic, 
and the control pot were all growing healthily and exponentially. However, later during the week 
it was discovered that the experiment had been tampered with and vandalized. The following 
week showed the effects of that as the 25 ml organic pot had died and been removed from the pot 
entirely to be replanted. The control pot was showing signs of environmental stress as 2.75 
inches broke off when it was touched. The part that had broken off was placed vertically in the 
pot in hopes that it would continue to grow or establish roots. During week 4, the leaves of the 
control pot were also showing signs of environmental stress. The leaves had developed 
brown/yellow spots, puzzling the researchers as they waited to observe further what the possible 
causes could be. The next week showed similar results as the control pot started shrinking and 
the texture of the leaves were dry and crusty. The researchers then made a collective decision to 
add new beans to observe whether the seeds would regrow as easily as they had before. 1 extra 
bean had been added to the pot labeled 25 ml organic, 2 for the 25 ml synthetic, and another 2 
extra beans for the 50 ml synthetic. Week 6 showed new results as there were signs of 2 new 
growths in the 50 ml organic and 1 new growth in the control pot. The new growths differed 
from the original observations, as they appeared to be sprouts with two little leaves opposite 
from each other compared to the original grows which had obviously sprouted from a seed. In 
the chart, the extra measurements below the original ones are the measurements of the new 
growths in inches. In the end, the original plant in the control pot had died and only the new 
growth remained. 
Analysis and Results 
The final day of observation showed evident differences between all of the plant growths. 
Although each plant was grown under the same control variable, including a 50:50 mixture of

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 10 
Martian soil stimulant and Earth soil, daily watering of 50 milliliters, and constant exposure to 
the ultraviolet light made the final outcomes vary significantly. Because all environmental 
factors were controlled, the changes in plant growth can be directly associated with the 
independent factor: the type and quantity of fertilizer used. The observations directly supported 
the hypothesis that different amounts of synthetic and organic fertilizers would affect the growth 
rates and lengths of green bean plants. It was seen that the disparity in outcomes followed the 
idea that the quantity and types of fertilizers played an important role in their development. 
In the control group, the pot without any fertilizer indicated stable but measured growth 
from the beginning to the end of the experiment. By the time the observation period came to an 
end, the control plant had already reached the height of nearly 8 ¾ inches and demonstrated 
constant development of the leaves and its sturdiness. This shows that green beans are capable of 
growing in a Martian soil mixture without any additional nutrients; however the growth is 
hindered when compared to plants that get further assistance. Therefore, the control group 
provided a reference point for comparison and revealed that, while the soil mixture could support 
life, it was still not ideal since it lacks sufficient nutrients to promote optimal growth. 
In comparison, the plants that were grown using the organic fertilizer demonstrated the 
highest level of growth and overall health performance. The plant with 25 milliliter of organic 
fertilizer achieved the greatest height, reaching approximately 12 inches, and displayed strong 
stems, flourishing healthy leaves, and a solid firm structure. The organic matter established a 
helpful growing environment by enhancing nutrient availability and supporting microbial 
activity. The plant that received 50 milliliter of organic fertilizer also grew efficiently, but it 
displayed signs of structural imbalance, featuring slight bending in the stems and fragile 
structure. These results show that organic fertilizer enhances plant growth, but too much may

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 11 
reduce optimal development and lead to nutrient imbalances or rapid growth, reducing overall 
structural stability. Overall, the organic fertilizer plants outperformed the control and synthetic 
ones, highlighting that soil chemicals are crucial for plant growth in nutrient-poor soil. 
 In contrast, the synthetic fertilizer plants had no measurable growth, given that neither 
plant achieved successful germination. Because of this, the 12% nitrogen in the synthetic 
fertilizer caused an excess of nitrogen, stunting the growth of the bean and causing a lack of 
germination. Comparatively, the organic fertilizer used, Mykos Pure Mycorrhizal Inoculant, 
contains “Rhizophagus intraradices” as an active ingredient. “Rhizophagus intraradices” are a 
type of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus. According to the University of Wisconsin-Madison 
Horticulture (2005), “Mycorrhizae are fungi that have a symbiotic relationship with the roots of 
many plants”. This symbiotic relationship creates a balanced exchange between the fungi and the 
plants. The plant produces carbon in which the fungi can feed off from, and the fungi act as a 
sponge to absorb excess nutrients for the plants, to then absorb and use to grow. These fungi are 
used in fertilizers as it can help promote root growth, expanding water and nutrient intake by 
wide margins and building stress tolerance. Mycorrhizae in soil is ideal for restoring degraded 
soil and accelerating growth through improving root structure. 
From these findings, it can be concluded that the reason both potted plants containing 25 
and 50 milliliters of synthetic fertilizer did not germinate was that they were ruined from the 
beginning. The excess amount of nitrogen delayed the growth compared to the pots containing 
organic fertilizer or none at all, producing no results. The control variable plant grew about 
average and if compared to the plants containing organic fertilizer, they set the standard for how 
green beans grow with no help other than watering them daily as a basic need. The pot with 25 
milliliter of organic fertilizer was the most successful until its unfortunate demise, during an act

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 12 
of vandalism. When compared to the pot with 50 milliliter of organic fertilizer, the 25 milliliter 
organic pot had more growth, with a stronger and thicker base connecting to the root. This is not 
to say that the 50 milliliter organic pot was not also successful, but when compared with the 25 
milliliter organic pot, the 50 milliliter organic pot showed that the 25 milliliter of organic 
fertilizer was a better ratio with the soil. Although all of the pots received the same amount of 
water, sunlight, and worms, the results show the effects of excess nitrogen and symbiotic fungi in 
fertilizer when applied to green beans. 
Conclusion 
The results agree with the hypothesis that different types and amounts of fertilizer are 
essential for plants to gain nutrients from and would promote beneficial soil activity and growth. 
The plant receiving 50 milliliters of organic fertilizer grew well and was able to maintain a 
structure throughout the duration of the experiment despite being tampered with. The control 
plant exhibited moderate growth, reaching 8 ¾ inches, showing that Martian soil along with the 
help of earth soil can support survival of the plants but not their optimal growth. In contrast, the 
synthetic fertilizer group failed to germinate, most likely due to excessive nitrogen interfering 
with the natural nitrogen fixation process in green beans. 
The environmental factors also influenced growth. Overwatering resulted in weak stems 
and overly mushy soil, leading to changing the tray every time the plants were watered. This 
factor also led to adding supports such as pencils and rolled papers to keep plants from 
drowning, and changing the napkin underneath the pots so the moisture wouldn’t cause growth 
of mold. Eventually plant stakes made for pots were added to replace the makeshift ones. These 
observations show that, in addition to fertilizer, careful management of water, soil structure, and 
plant support is important for successful growth under extreme conditions like Martian soil.

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 13 
If the experiment were repeated, specific improvements could enhance the results. 
Testing additional fertilizer concentrations could identify the most effective nutrient balance. 
Measuring soil pH, nutrient levels, and root development throughout the experiment would 
provide deeper insight into how fertilizer affects growth. Protecting the plants from damage and 
maintaining consistent environmental conditions would further improve the accuracy and 
reliability of the results. Overall, the results indicate that organic fertilizers combined with 
careful environmental management are critical for successful plant growth in Martian soil. These 
findings help understand how cultivating crops in challenging soils can support sustainable food 
production on long-duration missions. 
The observation of this experiment has important significance for future space 
exploration and long-term missions to Mars. Successfully growing green beans in a Martian soil 
stimulation demonstrates that, with the right combination of nutrients and environmental 
management, plants can serve as a reliable food source for astronauts. Organic fertilizers, which 
improve soil structure and support beneficial bacteria, are essential for maximizing growth in 
nutrient-poor soils. Continued research in this area can develop sustainable agricultural systems 
for space, reduce reliance on Earth-based food supplies, and ensure that astronauts have access to 
fresh nutritious crops during long-duration missions. This experiment confirms that plant growth 
in outer space environments is achieved, but relies heavily on careful nutrient management, 
monitoring the environment, and attentive care of the plants.

Ashley Kim, Alexis Magana, Wareesha Saeed 14
